title: Xenopoecilius oophorus (Beloniformes: Adrianichthyidae)

authors.affiliation: Department of Anatomy, Nippon Medical School, Sendagi 1-1-5, Bunkyo-ku, Tokyo 113, Japan

abstract_text: Xenopoecilius oophorus is a member of the basal clade of Adrianichthyidae. In order to determine the size and shape of brain regions in these fishes I used a 3-dimensional computer reconstruction system (TRI 3.10). To preserve the original size of structures specimens were immersion-fixed in 10% formalin and brains sectioned at 30 um on a cryostat. Outlines of 180 serial sections were traced to calculate the volume of one whole brain and six brain regions; olfactory bulbs (BO), telencephala (TE), optic tecta (TO), inferior lobes (IL), cerebellum (CE), and facial lobes (FL). Volumetric estimates from sampling every section were compared with estimates from sampling each 2nd, 4th and 8th section, as well as from ocular micrometry using linear measurements taken under a dissecting microscope. Estimates from section sampling and ocular micrometry did not differ significantly from the complete volumetric values. Estimates from ocular micrometry were derived from the ellipsoid model [V=1/6 pi*lwd] (l=length, w=width, and d=depth), except for the TO, which was estimated from [V=SA*T] (SA=surface area, T=thickness). Estimates of total brain size derived by measuring the linear distance between the anterior margin of the telencephalon and the obex did not differ significantly from estimates derived from weighing brains.

title: Pleomerism of vertebrae, fin rays, and scale rows in the gobiid fishes: observations and possible explanations

authors.affiliation: Severtsev Institute of Ecology and Evolution, Moscow 117071, Russia

abstract_text: According to Lindsey (1975), pleomerism is a correlation among related animal species between their numbers of meristic parts and their characteristic body sizes. Lindsey found a striking tendency for vertebral number to be positively correlated with maximum length in many families of fish; however, he did not find the same correlation among 36 species of the family Gobiidae in his analysis. Data on the maximum recorded size, numbers of vertebrae, fin-rays (in dorsal, anal, and pectoral fins), and scales in longitudinal row were taken from published reviews of the gobiid species occurring in the Indo-West-Pacific (120 species), South African (107), North East Atlantic (73), Black Sea (26) regions. Not only vertebral numbers, but all other counts appeared to be positively correlated with size of gobiid species in the four regions. Taxonomic applications of this phenomena and possible evolutionary explanations (e.g., life history correlates, structure of heritable morphological variation) are discussed.

title: Functional morphology of pectoral fin locomotion in basal actinopterygians

authors.affiliation: Department of Organismal Biology and Anatomy, University of Chicago, Chicago, IL 60637 USA
Department of Zoology, Field Museum of Natural History, Chicago, IL 60605 USA

abstract_text: Fishes use their pectoral fins for a variety of locomotor functions including providing thrust for rectilinear movement. Most previous analyses of pectoral fin swimming in fishes have focused on the Perciformes, a relatively derived group. In this study we examine pectoral fin swimming in Polypterus palmas, Lepisosteus platostomus, and Amia calva, representing three basal clades of ray-finned fishes. Both forward and reverse swimming are analyzed to reflect the wide range of behaviors during which fishes use their pectoral fins. Anatomical changes which have occurred in the pectoral fin complex include duplication of musculature and the formation of a specialized fin ray to act as the leading edge of the fin. Kinematically, the frequencies of fin beats and three-dimensional excursions of the fin differ greatly between species. Electromyograms reveal differences in the duration, relative timing, and amplitude of activity in the pectoral muscles suggesting that motor patterns during swimming are not highly conserved in these taxa. These data are compared with information from more derived taxa to trace the evolution of pectoral fin swimming in actinopterygians.

title: Geographic variation in the skeleton of the stoneroller, Campostoma anomalum

authors.affiliation: Museum of Biological Diversity, The Ohio State University, 1315 Kinnear Road, Columbus, OH 43212 USA

abstract_text: Comparative osteology of the nominal species Campostoma anomalum was investigated across most of its geographic range in North America. Considerable variation was found associated with the food cropping and food processing mechanisms (jaws, pharyngeals) and bones associated with the operation of these structures. Transformations in character states (using Campostoma ornatum and Dionda diaboli as outgroups) were found in the jaws, pharyngeals, suspensorium, opercular series, sphenotic, ethmoid, cranial roof and vertebral number. Results from the skeletal analysis were interpreted as follows. Two broadly defined groups were recognized. One, represented by Campostoma anomalum pullum, is widespread across the glaciated mid-section of North America and southward in the plains region. The second is a complex of forms (represented in the upper Ohio Valley by Campostoma a. anomalum) distributed in the Ohio River basin and peripheral areas to the east, south and west. The stonerollers found in the northern portions of the Ohio Valley can be pullum, anomalum or possible intermediates between the two depending on the drainage system. The largescale stoneroller, C. 'oligolepis', distributed in the Ozark uplands is a western component of the anomalum complex that is related to the similar but slightly more derived Tennessee-Cumberland stoneroller. The stoneroller that dominates the Tennessee-Cumberland is the most derived form of the anomalum complex. It has peripheral (extensions?) in the Green River, New River and on the gulf and east slopes. The name C. a. michauxi Fowler might apply to this form. Two of the most recognizable populations within the anomalum complex have smaller distributional ranges. One is found in the Roanoke-James and the other in the Ouachita drainage.

title: Sturgeons and their parasites: the historical biogeography of a host-parasite association

authors.affiliation: Department of Zoology, University of Toronto, Toronto, Ontario, M5S 3G5
Department of Zoology, University of Manitoba, Winnipeg

abstract_text: Sturgeons (Osteichthyes: Acipenseridae) are evolutionary relicts with a wide distribution in the northern hemisphere. The historical biogeography of their association with their diverse assemblage of host specific parasites is explored using phylogenetic systematics and information from geology, paleontology and paleogeography. The patterns indicate historical exchanges with a variety of host taxa and low levels of conspeciation, resulting in small clades of widely distributed parasite species. Sister taxa of parasites generally exhibit allopatric patterns associated with discrete landmasses and basins. A trans-Atlantic track involving Acipenser oxyrhynchus and A. sturio and a trans-Pacific track involving A. medirostris are evident. The parasite relationships also support a historical connection between North America and North Asian freshwater sturgeons (A. fulvescens and A. baeri or their ancestors) and the biogeographical and phylogenetic relationship of A. fulvescens and A. brevirostrum. Based on these parascript studies, it is hypothesized that a former contiguous distribution of Palaearctic and Nearctic sturgeons was fragmented by climatic and tectonic events in the Tertiary causing displacement of the lake sturgeon lineage and its association with the Gulf of Mexico drainages.

title: Biogeography of giant bacteria and their surgeonfish (Acanthuridae) hosts in the north Pacific

authors.affiliation: Department of Biological Sciences, Northern Arizona University, Flagstaff, Arizona, 86011-5640 USA
Department of Biological Sciences, Northern Arizona University, Flagstaff, Arizona, 86011-5640 USA
Department of Biological Sciences, Northern Arizona University, Flagstaff, Arizona, 86011-5640 USA
Department of Biological Sciences, Northern Arizona University, Flagstaff, Arizona, 86011-5640 USA
School of Biological Sciences, University of Auckland, Private Bag 92019, Auckland, New Zealand

abstract_text: Surgeonfishes harbor a group of gut symbionts that include the largest known Eubacteria (cell lengths of 30pm to >500pm). Because the bacteria are acquired after larval surgeonfishes settle from the plankton, the fish/symbiont system in the Hawaiian Archipelago and other north Pacific locations provides an opportunity to address questions about evolution of host and symbionts within and among hosts, within and among islands, and among island systems. We have surveyed microbes in host surgeonfishes from Hawaii, Maui, Oahu, Kauai, French Frigate Shoals, Pearl & Hermes, and Midway Islands in the Hawaiian Archipelago, as well as from the Red Sea, Great Barrier Reef, Tuvalu, Moorea (French Polynesia), Ishigaki Island (Japan) and Gulf of California. A variety of structural morphs of the bacteria, differing in maximum size, cell shape, and the number and mode of formation of daughter cells, have been recorded from all sites except the Gulf. There appears to be considerable consistency in morphs occupying particular host species among the Hawaiian islands, but little consistency among island systems in terms of morphs occupying given host species. Preliminary molecular studies suggest local divergence of microbes within a single host, at least for widely separated localities.

title: Parasites, life histories, mating systems

authors.affiliation: Department of Zoology, University of Toronto, 25 Harbord Street, Toronto, Ontario, M5S 3G5
Department of Zoology, University of Toronto, 25 Harbord Street, Toronto, Ontario, M5S 3G5
Department of Zoology, University of Toronto, 25 Harbord Street, Toronto, Ontario, M5S 3G5

abstract_text: Parasites may play an important role in fish life history and mating system evolution. This paper examines parasite loads in a natural colony of bluegill sunfish (Lepomis macrochirus). All 8 parasite-types were quantified in selected tissues of over 200 females, cuckolders and parentals (n=16,438 parasites). Females and cuckolders have fewer parasites than do parental males. Parental males that obtain nest sites within the colony have fewer parasites than unsuccessful parental males. Thus, parasites apparently determine parental male opportunity to breed, and sexual selection for delayed maturation in parental males increases their average parasite loads. The evolution of the mating system and life histories in this fish is therefore subject to forces of selection from parasites.

title: Sperm competition and the evolution of alternative male life histories

authors.affiliation: University of Toronto, 25 Harbord Street, Toronto, Ontario, M5S 3G5
University of Toronto, 25 Harbord Street, Toronto, Ontario, M5S 3G5
University of Toronto, 25 Harbord Street, Toronto, Ontario, M5S 3G5

abstract_text: Sperm competition is one vehicle by which males compete with each other for reproductive success. This paper examines sperm competition between the specialized cuckolder and parental male life histories of bluegill sunfish (Lepomis macrochirus). First, we find that the investment in total sperm production is higher in cuckolders than parentals and within cuckolders, males that have higher sperm production obtain higher fertilization success. Second, the longevity of sperm is lower in cuckolders than parentals. The alternative male reproductive life histories of bluegill therefore utilize sperm in different ways to compete for reproductive success. Cuckolders invest in quantity because they always face sperm competition, while parentals invest in quality because they only rarely face sperm competition. We compare these findings to those in other fishes by analyzing differences in sperm competition intensities and sperm quantity-quality tradeoffs.
